How Long Does Menopause Insomnia Last?

By Marian Grout, founder of 3:17 · Updated October 29, 2026

Short answer

SWAN research describes different night-waking patterns, including difficulties persisting into postmenopause; it does not establish one duration for everyone.[^1] For next steps, the NHS advises a medical review when sleep problems last months or make daily life hard to cope with.[^3]

In this article

  2. What does SWAN research tell us about night waking?

If you are awake again, wondering how many more nights like this lie ahead, I understand why you want a finish line. “How long does menopause insomnia last?” is a question about more than dates. You want to know what to expect, and what you can do next.

Is there a set number of months or years?

The longitudinal research discussed here does not establish one duration for menopause insomnia.[1] I wish I could give you a reliable countdown. I would rather be honest about the limits of the evidence than hand you a number to circle on the calendar.

The NHS describes perimenopause and menopause as different for everyone, with symptoms that can change over time.[6] That is a useful starting point when you are comparing your experience with a friend's. I would be cautious about turning anyone else's story into a deadline for your own.

For me, the useful question alongside “When will this end?” is “What should I ask about now?” You deserve a conversation that takes your nights seriously, even when there is no tidy answer about the future.

What does SWAN research tell us about night waking?

An earlier Study of Women's Health Across the Nation (SWAN) analysis collected women's sleep reports at baseline and seven annual assessments.[2] It found that the odds of difficulty falling asleep and staying asleep increased across the menopausal transition.[2]

A later SWAN analysis of women reaching menopause naturally identified four night-waking patterns: low, moderate, increasing and high.[1]

I would not use those groups to label you, or to decide in advance what your next year will look like. I read them as a reason to be wary of sweeping promises about what “all women” go through.

Another analysis, using ten years of SWAN data, found insomnia symptoms more prevalent in late than early perimenopause.[8] The symptoms measured in that analysis were self-reported.[8] Those ten years describe the study's data, rather than an average length of insomnia.[8] When a headline mentions a long follow-up, I always want to know exactly what the researchers measured before reading it as a personal forecast.

Will my sleep settle once my periods have stopped?

Repeated night waking could persist into postmenopause in the SWAN trajectory analysis.[1] That finding deserves a clear explanation, especially if you have been counting down to your last period.

The NHS describes menopause as having gone without a period for 12 months, followed by postmenopause.[6] I would use that definition to understand the terminology, without reading the anniversary as a promised date for better nights.

There is also a distinction between different sleep complaints: in the earlier SWAN analysis, the odds of early morning awakening decreased from late perimenopause to postmenopause.[2] I would want to tell a clinician exactly which experience I mean: struggling at bedtime, waking repeatedly, or waking too early and being unable to return to sleep.

You do not have to choose a perfect label before making an appointment. Your own words are a reasonable place to begin.

Do night sweats explain every difficult night?

The NHS notes that sleep problems may be worse when night sweats are also present.[6] In the earlier SWAN analysis, more frequent vasomotor symptoms were associated with higher odds of each sleep difficulty studied.[2]

I would mention heat and sweating if you notice them, rather than deciding beforehand how much they explain. Equally, I would describe a wakeful night without sweating exactly as it happened.

The NHS also lists stress, anxiety, depression and some medicines among causes of insomnia.[3] My preference would be to take a full account of the situation into the appointment, rather than arrive committed to a single explanation. Bring your questions; you do not need to bring your own diagnosis.

When should I talk to a clinician?

The NHS advises seeing a GP if sleep trouble has lasted months or makes daily life hard to cope with.[3] That is the guidance I would keep in mind if you are debating whether your experience is worth an appointment.

NHLBI defines chronic insomnia as occurring at least three nights weekly for three months or longer.[4] I would leave diagnosis to your clinician and use the dates and frequency as information to bring along.

I would also be specific about what “hard to cope with” means for you. Perhaps you are declining invitations, worrying about a workday, or finding ordinary responsibilities overwhelming. You do not have to make your account sound dramatic. Tell it plainly.

A sentence you could borrow is: “I keep waking during the night, and I want an assessment of my sleep as well as a conversation about menopause.” If you have already raised it, you can ask what the next step will be and when to follow up.

What care is worth asking about?

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine strongly recommends multicomponent cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, or CBT-I, for adults with chronic insomnia disorder.[5] Its guideline also suggests against using sleep hygiene alone for chronic insomnia disorder.[5]

That gives you a specific question for an appointment: “Would CBT-I be appropriate for me, and where could I access it?” I would ask about local availability, remote options, cost and what participation involves.

A randomized trial in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women with moderate insomnia symptoms and hot flashes found greater reductions in insomnia severity with telephone CBT-I than with menopause education.[7] The between-group differences were sustained at 24 weeks.[7]

I take that as a reason to ask about the option, without making a promise about any individual's result. Ask your clinician to explain which choices fit your circumstances and how you will review progress together. You are allowed to ask for a plain-language explanation.

What could I bring to the appointment?

NHLBI suggests keeping a sleep diary for one to two weeks before seeing a doctor.[4] Its suggested entries include sleep and wake times, naps, daytime sleepiness, caffeine, alcohol and exercise.[4]

My personal preference would be a simple notebook or a short note on my phone. I would keep the entries brief, use rough times where needed, and avoid turning the page into a test I could fail.

I would also write down three questions:

  • What would you like to assess before deciding on a plan?
  • Would CBT-I be appropriate, and how do I find it?
  • When should we review what happens next?

NHLBI says an assessment may include questions about medicines, menopause, loud snoring and waking gasping or short of breath.[4] If any of those apply, I would put them on the page rather than rely on remembering everything in the room.

If I had already tried several things, I would list them with a few words about my experience. I would bring the list as a record, without judging myself for how long it is.

What can I do with the uncertainty tonight?

My suggestion is to choose one small administrative step: draft the appointment request, put a notebook beside your bag, or write down the question you most want answered. Pick whichever feels manageable.

I would give myself permission to leave the research there for the evening. You do not owe anyone an exhaustive investigation before asking for care, and you do not have to solve the whole question tonight.

I cannot offer you a finish date. I can encourage you to take your experience seriously and ask for a clear next step. If sleep problems have lasted months, talk to a clinician.[3]

Questions women ask

Can night waking continue after menopause?

Repeated night waking could persist into postmenopause in the SWAN trajectory analysis.[^1] If sleep problems have lasted months, talk to a clinician.[^3]

Does menopause mean my sleep should settle after 12 months?

The NHS describes menopause as having gone without a period for 12 months, followed by postmenopause.[^6] I would not use that anniversary as a promised date for better nights.

When is insomnia considered chronic?

NHLBI defines chronic insomnia as occurring at least three nights weekly for three months or longer.[^4]

Should I wait until menopause is over to seek care?

The NHS advises seeing a GP if sleep trouble has lasted months or makes daily life hard to cope with.[^3] You can use that guidance when deciding about an appointment.

Is there CBT-I research in women going through menopause?

A randomized trial in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women with moderate insomnia symptoms and hot flashes found greater reductions in insomnia severity with telephone CBT-I than with menopause education.[^7] Ask your clinician whether CBT-I would be appropriate for you.
